overview: A single-page State Department file index or cross-reference sheet summarizing three communications concerning Japanese telecommunications between 1930 and 1933. The entries cover a proposal to transfer Japan’s state-operated telephone system to private ownership, the inauguration of direct telephone service between Tokyo and Keijo (Seoul), and International Telephone & Telegraph Corporation interest in radio-telephone and telephone links between Japan and South America.

people.name: Edwin L. Neville
people.role: U.S. diplomat in Japan; associated with Japan report or despatch no. 203

people.name: Frank C. Page
people.role: Correspondent associated with the International Telephone & Telegraph Corporation

subfiles.title: Index sheet on Japanese telephone services and international connections
subfiles.about: The sheet indexes three communications about telephone-system privatization, domestic and colonial telephone service, and communications between Japan and South America.
subfiles.summary: The first entry cites Japan report or despatch no. 203 of July 10, 1930, associated with Neville, concerning the Minister of Communications’ suggestion that Japan’s state-operated telephone system be transferred to private hands. It also notes that direct telephone service between Tokyo and Keijo opened on July 14, 1933, and cross-references Military Attaché Report no. 6894 of July 20, 1933. A final entry records a November 25 letter from Frank C. Page of the International Telephone & Telegraph Corporation and a related memorandum of conversation concerning radio-telephone and telephone connections between Japan and South America.

interest: This sheet is useful as a compact guide to several strands of Japan’s telecommunications history: proposed privatization of a state utility, the expansion of long-distance service within the Japanese Empire, and trans-Pacific commercial communications. Its reference to the Tokyo–Keijo circuit precisely dates an infrastructural connection between metropolitan Japan and colonial Korea, while the ITT entry points to private American corporate interest in Japan–South America links. As an index rather than the underlying correspondence, it also reveals how the State Department grouped and cross-referenced telecommunications intelligence.
